metadata.title: School Closure Policies and Student Reading Achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 microdata for fourth-grade reading achievement in 29 countries (with additional earlier PIRLS cycles for trend models). All analyses apply sampling weights; in pooled analyses, senate weights are used so that each country contributes equally to final estimates. Sampling variance is handled using jackknife repeated replication (JRR), consistent with PIRLS’ stratified class-based sampling design. The manuscript does not indicate any omission of weights; therefore, weighting is incorporated into the regression estimation rather than being ignored (unlike many ML-only pipelines).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that PIRLS reading achievement is estimated using a plausible value methodology and that analyses account for the five plausible values using Rubin’s rules. However, for missingness in student background controls (e.g., books at home, home language, computer access), the authors state that missing responses were coded as a separate missing category rather than describing a formal missing-data imputation strategy. Because the manuscript does not explicitly classify this approach as listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, or a specific imputation method, missing-data handling is treated as not fully reported for the schema.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample includes PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading assessments in 29 countries that participated in both rounds and for which UNESCO UIS data on school-closure duration were available. The study excludes countries where PIRLS 2021 was administered to a different grade level (e.g., fifth graders) to maintain comparability over time, and also excludes Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan because UIS does not provide school-closure-duration data for them. For heterogeneity analyses using the Home Resources for Learning scale, England is dropped because it did not administer the home questionnaire used to construct that scale. All models use sampling weights and jackknife repeated replication; missing background questionnaire items are coded as a separate missing category.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression coefficient for one additional day of school closures: -0.140 (S.E. 0.015), p<0.01; models use sampling (senate) weights and jackknife repeated replication; plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged school-closure duration alongside student controls (age, gender, books at home, home language, and computer access) to predict reading achievement change, finding that longer school closures were significantly associated with larger declines in reading performance (about -0.14 PIRLS scale points per additional day). This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 Reading (29 countries; heterogeneity models)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement change heterogeneity by home resources and computer access
main_findings.performance_metrics: Home resources interaction: Closed x Home Resources for Learning = 0.021 (S.E. 0.008), p<0.05; main Closed effect = -0.146 (S.E. 0.014), p<0.01. Computer interaction: No vs Yes baseline = -0.085 (S.E. 0.041), p<0.05. Language and gender interactions not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged interactions between school-closure duration and student background (home resources, computer access, home language, and gender) to predict reading achievement change, finding that the negative effect of closures was more pronounced for socioeconomically disadvantaged students and those without home computer access. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study combines PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade reading achievement data with UNESCO UIS measures of national school-closure duration across 29 countries. Using sampling (senate) weights and jackknife repeated replication, and combining PIRLS plausible values via Rubin’s rules, the authors estimate that one additional day of school closures is associated with a -0.14 PIRLS scale-point decline in reading achievement between 2016 and 2021 (S.E. 0.015). The effect is robust across alternative specifications (global trends and country-specific trends) and robustness checks excluding delayed-wave countries, excluding federal decentralized countries, and varying the weighting of partially closed days. Heterogeneity analyses show that the negative association is attenuated for students with higher Home Resources for Learning and is more negative for students without a computer at home, while gender and home language differences are not statistically significant. The paper is regression-based rather than ML-based, so no ML model performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) are reported.
